question.problem: What are the solutions of the equation $6{y}^{2}+14=0?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{y}^{2}+14 & =0 \\ 6{y}^{2} & =-14 \\ {y}^{2} & =-\frac{14}{6} \\ {y}^{2} & =-\frac{7}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

By taking square root, we obtain:

$$
y=\pm \sqrt{-\frac{7}{3}}
$$

We now rewrite $y$ using the imaginary unit $\text{i}=\sqrt{-1}\,:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\pm \sqrt{-\frac{7}{3}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{7}{3}\cdot (-1)} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{7}{3}}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{3}}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rationalize the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{3}}\text{i} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \sqrt{-1} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{21}}{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$
